newsitem.title: ITALY: De Benedetti's CIR gains on Valeo sale.
newsitem.headline: De Benedetti's CIR gains on Valeo sale.

text.p: Shares in Carlo De Benedetti holding Compagnie Industriali Riunite SPA (CIR), which holds 14 percent of the troubled Olivetti group, spiked up nine percent in Milan at one stage on Tuesday news it was selling its stake in French car parts manufacturer Valeo. The shares later showed gains of some 3.6 percent.

CIR, which through its holding Cerus held 27.44 percent in car parts firm Valeo, quickly pared gains to stand 3.62 percent up by 1450 GMT at 749 lire on the announcement it was selling the stake at 330 French francs per share to CGIP, Morgan GT Corp and French state-owned bank CDC.
CIR hit a low of 606 lire on October 22, not far above its record low set in September this year during a crisis in the top management ranks of Olivetti.
Since late October CIR has climbed steadily with the market expecting Valeo negotiations following widespread press reports.
Marco Nascimbeni, head of equity trading operations at Carnegie in Milan, said the news had mostly been discounted. "The only unknown thing was the price."
"Now the question is what will it do with the money. There will be a reduction of debt but there is also liquidity which could be used for doing something else," he said.
CIR said in a statement that Cerus' sale of the stake would bring CIR a capital gain of 550 billion lire.

"In the framework of the operation...CIR improves its own net consolidated financial position by 1.94 trillion lire, before the capital reimbursement taking place in the first quarter of 1997 for more than 1.0 trillion, of which 500 billion pertains to CIR," the statement said.

"The total effect of the operation brings a drastic improvement in CIR's financial structure and represents a decisive step in realising the objective of reducing its financial debt to zero," the statement said.

"If I had to chose between Cerus and CIR as to where to put my money, I'd chose Cerus because that's the company which has the cash earning. It's cutting debts, and after a revaluation it also has other stakes in its portfolio," another broker said.
"Also if one company was to pay a dividend it would be more likely to be Cerus and not CIR because Cerus had the cash earning," he added.
"If you're taking a view of the De Benedetti-Olivetti group, on the whole it's positive although there is no impact for Olivetti or Cofide, it's just for CIR."
"Longer term for CIR this is neutral. It gets the cash earning now but Valeo was an alright company even if it wasn't big business," he added.

Nascimbeni said the biggest problem for the De Benedetti group as a whole still remained information technology group Olivetti and the Valeo sale would have little impact on the market's perception of the group.
"Before thinking about a rally in the Olivetti share price the company has to deliver results," Nascimbeni said.
